settings.question: How much does tire rotation cost?
settings.answer: Tire rotation costs a flat $60 at Prince Tires for most vehicles — cars, SUVs, vans, EVs and pickups — and $100 for dual-rear-wheel (dually) and heavy-duty trucks. No hidden shop fees. You'll see the exact price when you book online.

settings.question: How often should I rotate my tires in Alberta?
settings.answer: Every 8,000 to 12,000 km is the general rule — roughly every other oil change. Alberta driving is hard on even wear: long dry highway runs on the QE2, gravel shoulders, and winter roads all wear the front tires faster. The easy way to remember it in Calgary is to have the rotation done at your seasonal tire changeover, spring and fall.

settings.question: Why does rotating tires matter?
settings.answer: Front tires carry the steering and most of the braking load, so they wear faster than the rears. Left alone, you'd replace the fronts long before the rears are worn out. Rotating on a regular pattern evens out the wear, so you get the full life from all four and replace them as a set.

settings.question: Do I still need rotation if I run separate winter and summer tires?
settings.answer: Yes. Swapping seasonal sets isn't the same as rotating — each set still wears unevenly front-to-rear over its own season. We can rotate each set as part of the changeover; just ask when you book.

settings.question: How long does a tire rotation take?
settings.answer: About 30 minutes for most vehicles. Book a slot online, drop the vehicle, and you're back on the road quickly — same-day service is usually available.

settings.question: Rotation vs balancing — what's the difference?
settings.answer: Rotation moves each tire to a different position on the vehicle so the tread wears evenly — that's the $60 service on this page. Balancing adds small weights to the wheel so it spins true, which is what fixes a vibration in the steering wheel at highway speed. They're separate services: tire balancing is $20 per wheel, and we can do both in the same visit.

settings.heading: Tire Rotation Service Calgary
settings.subheading: Front tires wear out faster than rears — a lot faster. Our tire rotation service in Calgary moves each tire to a new position so all four wear evenly and last longer. $60 flat, about 30 minutes, same-day at our SW Calgary shop.

Your front and rear tires don't wear at the same rate: the fronts handle steering and most of the braking, so they wear faster. settings.text: Every turn scrubs the front tires sideways across the pavement. The rears just follow.

settings.lead: The fronts do most of the braking
settings.text: Weight shifts forward under braking, so the front tires carry a larger share of the load exactly when the load is highest.

settings.lead: On front-wheel drive they also pull
settings.text: Steering, most of the braking, and all of the power through the same two tires. Fronts can wear roughly twice as fast as rears.

settings.lead: Uneven wear costs a whole set
settings.text: Left alone you replace two tires while the other two still have tread, then the set is mismatched from then on. Rotation spreads the wear so all four finish together.

settings.heading: Why front and rear tires wear at different rates
settings.intro: On most vehicles the front tires do more work than the rears, and the gap is larger than people expect.
settings.outro: Rotation is a flat $60 for most vehicles and about 30 minutes. Book a rotation or call (403) 452-4283.

settings.text: Fronts go straight back. Rears cross to the opposite front corner.
The mirror image — rears go straight forward, fronts cross to the opposite rear.
Usually a full cross. AWD is least tolerant of mismatched tread depth, because a difference between axles makes the centre differential work continuously.
An arrow on the sidewall means the tread only works one way. Those rotate front-to-back on the same side, or the tire has to come off the rim to change sides.

settings.lead: Staggered fitments may not rotate at all
settings.text: If the rear tires are a wider size than the fronts, there is nowhere for them to go. Common on performance cars and some trucks.

settings.heading: Rotation patterns, and the tires that cannot be crossed
settings.intro: There is no single pattern. The right one depends on the drivetrain and on the tires themselves — getting it wrong is worse than not rotating.
settings.outro: Running separate winter and summer sets does not replace rotation — each set still wears unevenly over its own season. Ask for it with your seasonal changeover.

settings.text: The inner or outer edge going bald while the rest looks fine points to an alignment angle, not to tire position. Rotating just moves the problem to a different corner.

settings.lead: Feathering you can feel across the tread
settings.text: Run a hand across the tread. Smooth one way and sharp the other usually means a toe angle is off.
Dips around the circumference usually mean worn shocks or struts letting the tire bounce.

settings.lead: Centre worn, or both edges worn
settings.text: A strip down the middle means over-inflation. Both shoulders means under-inflation — easy to reach in Calgary, where pressure drops 1–2 PSI for every 5°C.
The moulded bars sit at 1.6 mm. Level with the tread means the tire is legally worn out and rotation is not the answer.

settings.heading: When rotation will not fix the wear
settings.intro: Rotation evens out normal wear. It does not correct a cause, and some wear patterns are telling you something else is wrong.
settings.outro: Alignment is a separate service and not one we perform — if the wear pattern points that way, we will tell you rather than rotate around it.
